1.title: Know the words of graphic design
1.intro: Graphic design uses shapes, type, colour and images to send a clear message.
pts: Learn the terms: layout, grid, typeface, hierarchy, contrast, margin, vector, raster, resolution, RGB, CMYK.
Raster images are made of pixels; vector images are made of lines and can be enlarged without blur.
RGB is for screens; CMYK is for print.
Look at five posters and name the headline, image, text and call to action.
1.ex: A poster has a big headline, one image and a small date line. The eye goes headline, image, date.
1.act: Mark hierarchy, contrast and alignment on five designs.
1.std: Task: analyse five designs. Condition: with printed or saved samples. Standard: all parts labelled and one improvement named for each.

2.title: Explain a design job from brief to files
2.intro: A job has steps. Name them to plan your time.
pts: The steps: brief, research, sketches, first design, feedback, changes, final files.
A brief states purpose, audience, size, where it will be used, deadline and the one action wanted.
Ask for text, logos and images before you start.
Agree how many rounds of changes are included.
2.ex: A client wants a flyer. You ask: Who reads it? Where is it handed out? What size? What must it say?
2.act: Write a brief form and test it on a friend.
2.std: Task: complete a brief. Condition: 30-minute conversation. Standard: purpose, audience, size, use, deadline and change rounds are stated.

3.title: Design a clear piece to a standard
3.intro: Now you make. Use layout, type and colour to guide the reader.
pts: Put the main point first and make it the biggest.
Use two typefaces at most and one clear colour scheme.
Leave white space; do not fill every corner.
Check contrast so text can be read, including by people with low vision.
3.ex: Before: five fonts, crowded text. After: one headline font, one body font, 20 mm margins, strong contrast.
3.act: Design a flyer and a social post from one brief, with three sketches first.
3.std: Task: design a flyer and a post. Condition: from a written brief in four hours. Standard: clear hierarchy, readable contrast, correct size and no spelling errors.

4.title: Follow Canadian rules for design work
4.intro: Design touches copyright, advertising and accessibility rules.
pts: Copyright protects images, fonts, music and logos. Use your own work or licensed work and keep the licence; check the current rule with the local authority.
Typefaces have licences. Check what your licence allows before using one in a client job.
Advertising must be truthful. Some products, such as alcohol, food and health, have extra rules; check the current rule with the local authority.
In Quebec, commercial signage and advertising generally need French; check the current rule with the local authority. Accessibility rules can apply to public documents.
4.ex: A client wants a photo from a web search. You say it may be protected and offer a licensed or original image.
4.act: Make a table of rule, who sets it, what you must do and where you checked, for ten design situations.
4.std: Task: build a rules table. Condition: using official public pages. Standard: each row has a dated source; unclear items say 'check the current rule with the local authority'.

5.title: Price your design work and check it pays
5.intro: You are paid for results and time. Know your real cost per hour.
pts: Time includes briefing, sketches, drafts, changes and file preparation.
Hourly cost = yearly costs plus needed pay, divided by billable hours.
Compare hourly, per-piece and per-project pricing.
Software and licences are costs; count them.
5.ex: A logo takes 10 hours at 50 USD: 500 USD, plus 8 USD for fonts. Teaching figures only.
5.act: Time three jobs and set a price for each.
5.std: Task: price three jobs. Condition: from your own time log. Standard: hours, rate and total are shown and a mentor can follow every number.

6.title: Prepare files, find clients and show proof
6.intro: Clients buy from designers they trust, and good files save everyone time.
pts: Export the right formats: PDF for print, PNG or JPG for screens, vector for logos.
Name files clearly, for example client_project_version_date.
Build a portfolio of five pieces with a brief and result beside each.
Contact ten local businesses with a specific idea for each; keep a log.
6.ex: You tell a bakery: 'Your menu board is hard to read from the door. Here is a quick redesign.'
6.act: Build a portfolio and send ten tailored messages.
6.std: Task: run a two-week outreach. Condition: consent-based contact and permission to show work. Standard: ten messages sent, replies logged and a lesson written.

7.title: Protect ownership, files and quality
7.intro: A professional designer is careful with rights and checks.
pts: Write who owns the final design and what the client may do with it. Ask a legal adviser for large deals.
Keep source files safe and backed up.
Check text, names, prices, dates and links before delivery.
Test print files with a small proof when possible.
7.ex: Your agreement says: 'The client owns the final artwork once paid in full. The designer may show it in a portfolio.'
7.act: Write an agreement template and a final check list.
7.std: Task: produce a template and checklist. Condition: reviewed by a mentor. Standard: scope, fees, rounds, rights and payment dates are in plain words.

8.title: Run a real design practice for 60 days
8.intro: Now you run it: take jobs, measure and decide.
pts: Set a goal such as three paid jobs and one repeat client.
Record hours, income, changes asked for and late items each week.
Ask each client for feedback.
Choose: stop, change or grow, and write a 12-month plan.
8.ex: After 60 days: 3 clients, 28 hours, 1,300 USD billed. You raise your rate and limit change rounds.
8.act: Run the pilot and present a 12-month plan to a panel of three.
8.std: Task: run a 60-day pilot. Condition: real clients and agreements. Standard: log complete and the decision uses numbers.

quiz: What is the difference between raster and vector?
Raster uses pixels; vector uses lines and scales without blur.
Which colour mode is for screens and which for print?
RGB for screens, CMYK for print.
What is visual hierarchy?
The order in which the eye reads the parts.
Why check contrast?
So text is easy to read, including for low vision.
What does a brief state?
Purpose, audience, size, use, deadline and change rounds.
Why check font licences?
They limit how a typeface may be used.
Why show a flaw-free portfolio with briefs?
It shows your thinking and results.
What file formats go to print and screen?
PDF for print; PNG or JPG for screens.
What do you check before delivery?
Text, names, prices, dates, links and file formats.
What do you do when you do not know a rule?
Check the current rule with the local authority.
